strengths: Addresses an important and practical vision/design problem: editing text in images while controlling font from visual glyph references, including multiple regions with different styles.

The proposed conditioning setup is simple and plausible: target-content reference image plus glyph-reference map are encoded and concatenated into the diffusion input, which is a reasonable way to inject both layout/content and font style without relying on font labels.

The paper evaluates beyond a single custom dataset, including an in-house poster benchmark, AnyText English/Chinese benchmarks, and handwritten text-line generation datasets, which helps support the claim that the approach generalizes across text styles and scripts.

Quantitative results are strong across many reported metrics. On the SkyReels-Text benchmark it improves style adherence substantially over baselines, and on AnyText it reports clear gains in FID/LPIPS and Chinese/English text accuracy over FLUX-Text and other specialized methods.

Qualitative comparisons are compelling in several cases: the method often preserves background structure and transfers decorative or handwritten font appearance better than general-purpose image editors.

The paper includes useful ablations for font style reference and text-region weighted loss, showing that the reference condition improves DINO style similarity and spatial alignment, and that region weighting improves text fidelity.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is moderate. The core model appears to be Qwen-Image-Edit fine-tuned with LoRA while adding VAE-encoded reference images/glyph maps and a spatially weighted loss. This is effective, but many ingredients are borrowed from existing diffusion editing, glyph conditioning, and distillation methods; the manuscript should more clearly separate engineering integration from new algorithmic contribution.

The comparison protocol is not fully convincing. Several baselines are general-purpose or do not natively accept the same visual font reference condition, so it is unclear whether failures reflect weaker models or an unfair interface mismatch. Details on prompts, masks, reference inputs, sampling steps, and whether baselines received comparable font information are insufficient.

The main in-house SkyReels-Text benchmark has only 200 samples and is not described in enough detail to assess diversity, difficulty, annotation quality, or possible overlap with training data. This weakens the central poster-editing evidence.

Font-style fidelity is mostly measured with DINO similarity, which is only a proxy and may conflate texture, color, layout, or background preservation with typography. There is no human preference/user study, no font-recognition/style-classification metric, and limited analysis of failure cases such as very long strings, curved text, occlusion, perspective, low resolution, or scripts beyond English/Chinese.

The data-generation pipeline is under-specified and potentially circular. Training pairs are produced using editing models and filtered using the authors' VLM OCR and DINO similarity, while evaluation also relies heavily on OCR and DINO-like metrics. This raises concern that the model may learn artifacts of the synthetic editing pipeline and that evaluation may favor the same filtering assumptions.

Ablations are too limited for the number of claimed components. There is no clear ablation of the VLM-based OCR data curation, content-style decoupling strategy, use of real poster data versus synthetic data, frozen VAE feature concatenation versus alternative conditioning, LoRA rank, distillation quality/speed tradeoff, or multi-font editing specifically.

The FSR ablation shows a substantial drop in sentence accuracy and NED when font style reference is enabled, despite better DINO score. The explanation attributes this partly to OCR difficulty, but this is not validated; it could also indicate that style control degrades legibility.

Reproducibility is weak. The paper does not specify whether the curated dataset, benchmark, OCR annotations, code, trained model, and evaluation scripts will be released. Important implementation details for data collection, licensing, masks, glyph crop construction, reference-map rendering, commercial API settings, and DMD2 distillation are missing.

The manuscript contains several clarity and polish issues, including grammatical errors, inconsistent terminology such as “edition,” ambiguous claims like operating without training/fine-tuning despite requiring substantial training, and incomplete reporting of some results such as speedup details for the distilled model. These are mostly presentation issues but they make some claims harder to verify.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important problem: editing text in poster-like images while controlling font/style from visual references, including multi-region and multilingual cases.

The proposed conditioning setup is simple and plausible: using a reference poster/content stream plus a glyph/style stream through frozen VAE features, combined with a text-region weighted loss, is an understandable extension of a strong editing backbone.

The experiments cover several relevant settings: an in-house poster benchmark, AnyText English/Chinese benchmarks, and handwriting-style transfer datasets. Reported numbers are often competitive or state-of-the-art, especially on Chinese AnyText and the DINO style metric.
Qualitative examples show that the method can preserve background content and transfer stylized typography better than several general-purpose image editing systems in the displayed cases.
weaknesses: The core technical novelty appears limited. The method mainly fine-tunes Qwen-Image-Edit with LoRA, concatenates VAE-encoded visual conditions, and applies a spatially weighted reconstruction loss. These are reasonable engineering choices, but the manuscript does not convincingly distinguish the contribution from prior glyph-conditioned or reference-conditioned text editing approaches.

The inference-time font-control mechanism is underspecified and somewhat inconsistent. The paper claims users can provide cropped glyph patches from arbitrary fonts, but the method describes rendering corresponding glyphs onto a blank canvas. It is unclear how arbitrary target characters are rendered in a font when only a visual crop/reference is available, especially for unseen characters or scripts.

The data pipeline is a major unresolved concern. Training pairs are produced using OCR, Qwen3-generated replacements, and unspecified editing models, then filtered by the authors' VLM OCR and DINO similarity. This creates possible circularity and inherited artifacts, yet there is little detail on annotation quality, filtering thresholds, data sources, legal status, or failure cases.

Evaluation is not sufficiently convincing for the strength of the claims. The main SkyReels-Text benchmark is only 200 samples, in-house, and not described in enough detail to judge difficulty, diversity, or leakage. There is no human evaluation for typography/style fidelity, which is central to the paper's claimed professional design use case.

Comparison fairness is unclear. Commercial/general editing models may not receive equivalent masks, glyph references, prompts, or constraints, and the prompting/settings are not reported. The 'Baseline' in Table 2 is also poorly defined, making it difficult to isolate gains from architecture, data, or backbone fine-tuning.

The ablation evidence is weak. Removing the Font Style Reference improves sentence accuracy and NED substantially, while the paper explains this away via OCR limitations. The ablation does not separately test the reference poster stream, glyph map stream, OCR/data pipeline, distillation, or LoRA choices, so the source of improvement remains uncertain.

Several claims are overreaching relative to the evidence, including 'unprecedented control,' 'professional-grade typographic design,' and strong generalization to handwriting. The handwriting comparison appears to mix a poster text editing model with dedicated handwriting generation models under potentially different task assumptions.

Reproducibility is poor. The manuscript reports compute and some optimizer details, but omits many essential details: exact training data construction, prompts, masks, OCR training targets, distillation setup/results, inference latency, baseline configurations, benchmark release plans, and whether model/data/code will be available.

Presentation has many grammar and precision issues, and some terminology is confusing, e.g., 'single-font edition,' 'text to be edited within region with reference glyph,' and inconsistent naming of Nano Banana/Gemini. These are not the main reason for rejection, but they compound the technical ambiguity.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and practical gap: font-controllable text editing in poster/design images, where both spelling fidelity and typographic style preservation matter. The task is well motivated and clearly distinct from generic image editing or text rendering.

The proposed conditioning design is simple and appealing: using user-provided glyph patches plus a reference edited poster/map gives explicit visual control without requiring font labels or per-font fine-tuning. This is potentially useful for real design workflows, especially for custom or ornamental fonts.

Empirical results are strong across several settings. The method improves over commercial and open-source baselines on the SkyReels-Text benchmark, AnyText English/Chinese metrics, and handwritten generation metrics, while qualitative examples show visibly better style transfer and text preservation in many cases.

The paper includes meaningful ablations for the font-style reference and text-region weighted loss, and the results support the claim that explicit font reference improves style adherence and spatial alignment.

The scope is broader than standard poster editing: the evaluation includes multilingual scene text and handwriting-style transfer, suggesting good generalization of the visual font-reference mechanism.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is limited. The main training data are 100k curated/generated poster pairs, but the paper gives few concrete details about data sources, filtering thresholds, replacement generation, prompts, editing model settings, licensing, or whether the data/model/code will be released. This makes the central empirical pipeline hard to reproduce.

The data generation process is somewhat circular and under-specified: the ground-truth edited images are produced using existing editing models, then filtered by the authors' VLM OCR and DINO similarity. It is unclear how errors or stylistic biases from these teacher/editing models affect training and evaluation.

Evaluation of font/style fidelity relies heavily on DINO similarity and qualitative inspection. For a design-oriented task, a human preference study or more direct typography/style metric would substantially strengthen the claims, especially for ornamental fonts where OCR and feature metrics may be unreliable.

The in-house SkyReels-Text benchmark has only 200 samples and appears private. Since this benchmark is central to the font-controllable poster-editing claim, its limited size and unavailable composition reduce confidence in the reported gains.

The baseline comparison protocol is not fully clear. For commercial/general image editing models, the prompts, reference usage, number of attempts, and whether models received the same glyph-reference information are not sufficiently specified, which may affect fairness.

The VLM-based OCR system is claimed as a contribution, but its own quantitative evaluation is missing. Since the same OCR/VLM machinery is used for dataset construction and possibly evaluation, its accuracy and potential bias should be reported.

The distillation component is described but not evaluated in detail. The paper claims over 10x speedup and quality preservation, yet no latency table, step-quality tradeoff, or teacher-vs-student comparison is provided.

Some presentation and technical details are imprecise: the method equation uses image-space notation for a diffusion loss, the reference poster generation step is ambiguous at inference time, and several grammatical/formatting issues make parts of the manuscript harder to parse. These are fixable but currently obscure implementation details.

strengths: The paper targets an important and practical gap: controllable poster/text editing where the user can specify arbitrary visual font references rather than choosing from labeled font libraries or relying on text prompts. This is well motivated for design workflows and is meaningfully different from generic image editing or OCR-guided text rendering.

The proposed conditioning design is simple and plausible: a plain-text layout image provides content and geometry, while a separate glyph/style map provides font appearance, both encoded with a frozen VAE and concatenated with the noisy latent in a Qwen-Image-Edit/DiT backbone. This is technically reasonable and likely to be useful in practice.

The data pipeline is a notable contribution. The manuscript describes a VLM-based OCR system for ornate fonts, LLM-based replacement text generation, local editing, SAM2 masks, and OCR/DINO verification to build 100K content-style decoupled pairs. The supplementary OCR benchmark and statistics add helpful support.

Empirical results are broad across an in-house poster benchmark, AnyText English/Chinese, handwritten IAM/CVL, qualitative comparisons, and a user study. Reported gains are especially strong on style adherence and AnyText FID/LPIPS, and the qualitative examples support the claimed advantage over general-purpose editors.
The paper is generally clear, with readable figures and enough implementation details to understand the training recipe, compute cost, LoRA setup, loss weighting, and evaluation metrics.
weaknesses: The strongest results depend heavily on non-public or closed components and data sources: Qwen-Image-Edit, Nano Banana/Gemini, commercial baselines, design-platform images, and an in-house SkyReels-Text benchmark. The abstract claims code/models are available, but the link is blank in the manuscript. As written, reproducibility is limited.

Evaluation has a circularity risk. The same fine-tuned Qwen2.5-VL OCR family is used in dataset construction/verification and also for key text-fidelity metrics on the SkyReels-Text benchmark. This can bias the reported sentence accuracy, NED, and spatial IoU toward the proposed pipeline, especially for ornate fonts where OCR behavior is central.

The in-house SkyReels-Text benchmark contains only 200 samples, and details of its construction, split independence from training data, font/style distribution, prompt protocol, and whether commercial baselines received equivalent reference inputs are not sufficiently specified. This weakens the central poster-editing evidence.

The novelty is partly engineering integration rather than a fundamentally new modeling technique. VAE feature concatenation, LoRA fine-tuning, text-region weighting, OCR filtering, and DMD-style distillation are sensible, but individually familiar; the paper should be judged mainly on system effectiveness and dataset contribution.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence. The paper states “unprecedented control,” “professional-grade,” and “state-of-the-art” broadly, but the comparisons are uneven across task settings, with several baselines not naturally designed for arbitrary font-reference editing. The handwritten results are interesting but are somewhat tangential to poster text editing.

The ablation evidence is thin. Font Style Reference improves DINO but substantially lowers OCR text accuracy relative to no-FSR, and the explanation is not fully satisfying. There is no detailed ablation of the two conditioning streams, glyph-map construction, dataset verification thresholds, OCR quality, distillation quality/speed tradeoff, or multi-region editing robustness.

The distillation section claims over 10x speedup and 8-step inference, but the main experiments do not clearly separate teacher vs. distilled student quality, sampling steps, runtime comparisons, or failure cases. This makes the efficiency claim under-supported.

Data provenance and licensing are insufficiently discussed. The method uses posters from design platforms such as Pinterest and Amazon plus generated edits from commercial models; for a dataset/model release, this raises important reproducibility, copyright, and redistribution questions that the manuscript does not resolve.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important and under-served problem: editing poster text while controlling typography from a visual reference, including multi-region and multi-font cases. This is a relevant contribution area for image editing and design workflows.

The proposed conditioning setup is simple and plausible: a plain-text layout image supplies content/layout while a glyph/style map supplies typographic appearance, both encoded by a frozen VAE and injected into a Qwen-Image-Edit backbone via LoRA. This is likely useful engineering even if not conceptually radical.

The manuscript reports a reasonably broad set of experiments, including an in-house poster benchmark, AnyText, IAM/CVL handwriting datasets, ablations, qualitative comparisons, and a user preference study. The qualitative examples suggest the method can produce visually convincing edits in some poster-like cases.

The data pipeline recognizes a real bottleneck: paired font-controlled text-editing data are hard to obtain, and the attempt to decouple text content and style through OCR, LLM replacement, local editing, segmentation, and verification is a potentially useful recipe.
weaknesses: The empirical case is not sufficiently trustworthy for the strength of the claims. The primary SkyReels-Text benchmark has only 200 in-house samples, and key metrics such as sentence accuracy, NED, and spatial IoU are computed using the authors' own fine-tuned OCR model. This creates a serious risk of evaluator bias, especially because the OCR model is also part of the data-generation and verification pipeline.

The evaluation of font fidelity is weak. DINO similarity between generated and reference text regions is a coarse proxy and may reward texture/color/background similarity rather than true typographic matching. The paper does not include human or font-recognition-based style metrics targeted at glyph shape, stroke width, kerning, or style consistency.

The ablation results undercut the central claim more than the paper acknowledges. Adding the Font Style Reference raises DINO but substantially lowers Sen. Acc. from 0.9327 to 0.8334 and NED from 0.9734 to 0.9502 on the main benchmark. This suggests that font control introduces a large text-fidelity cost, yet the paper still frames the approach as achieving precise text editing.

The novelty appears mostly incremental: the method combines a strong existing editing model, LoRA fine-tuning, VAE-encoded visual conditions, OCR/LLM-generated training pairs, SAM2 masks, DINO filtering, and DMD2 distillation. These are reasonable components, but the manuscript does not clearly isolate a technically novel mechanism beyond the particular assembly.

Several important implementation details are underspecified. It is unclear how arbitrary user glyph crops are normalized into the glyph map, how plain-text references are rendered/inpainted, how masks and red-box prompts are produced at inference, what exact prompts/settings are used for competing commercial models, and how multi-font references are ordered and associated with regions.

The baselines and task definitions are not always fair or well matched. Public AnyText metrics evaluate general text synthesis/editing rather than the paper's claimed font-reference control, while commercial baselines may be disadvantaged by insufficiently specified multi-reference prompting. The manuscript states FLUX-Pro is omitted in multi-font editing because it cannot process multiple reference images, but this does not fully establish fair comparison for the method's intended inputs.

Reproducibility is poor. The abstract says code and models are publicly available but the link is blank in the provided manuscript. The training relies on 512 A100-hours, a fine-tuned Qwen2.5-VL OCR model, Nano Banana-generated edits, SAM2/DINO filtering, and data collected from Pinterest/Amazon, but release details, licenses, prompts, thresholds beyond a few values, and dataset access are insufficient for independent reproduction.

The data construction raises unresolved validity and legal/ethical concerns. The training data include publicly accessible Pinterest and Amazon images and edited outputs from a proprietary/local editing system, but the paper does not discuss licensing, redistribution rights, consent, or whether benchmark/training overlap with public evaluation images is controlled.

The user study is not adequately documented. The paper reports preference rates but gives no number of participants, number of trials, randomization/blinding protocol, interface, statistical uncertainty, or criteria shown to raters. As a result, it is hard to use the study as strong evidence.

The claimed 10x speedup from DMD2 distillation is not supported by a table of latency, hardware, sampling steps for baselines, or quality trade-offs. Distillation is presented as a component but not evaluated with the same rigor as the main model.

The paper's wording is often stronger than the evidence supports, using phrases such as 'unprecedented control', 'professional-grade', and 'state-of-the-art' despite reliance on private benchmarks, proxy metrics, and incomplete reproducibility.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and practical problem in image editing: accurately replacing poster text while preserving fine-grained typography, layout, and background consistency. This is a real gap in current general-purpose image editing models.

The proposed dual-stream visual conditioning design is well motivated. Separating a plain-text layout/content condition from a glyph/style reference gives the model explicit signals for both spelling and font transfer, and the approach is simpler than heavier ControlNet-style conditioning.

The paper provides broad empirical evidence across several settings: an in-house poster benchmark, AnyText English/Chinese benchmarks, handwritten IAM/CVL evaluations, comparisons to both open-source and commercial systems, qualitative examples, and a user study.

The results are strong overall. SkyReels-Text improves text accuracy, style similarity, perceptual quality, and user preference in most reported comparisons, and the handwritten zero-shot results suggest useful generalization beyond the poster domain.

The data pipeline is a meaningful contribution. The authors identify the content-style entanglement problem and propose a reasonably systematic generation and filtering procedure using OCR, LLM replacement, local editing, SAM2 masks, DINO similarity, and verification thresholds.

The supplementary material improves credibility by reporting OCR dataset construction details, annotation scale, filtering criteria, OCR benchmark comparisons, and thresholds used for content/style verification.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is a significant concern. The abstract claims code and models are publicly available, but the URL is blank in the manuscript. The pipeline also depends on commercial or closed systems such as Nano Banana and comparisons to proprietary models, making exact replication difficult.

The evaluation partly relies on the authors' own fine-tuned OCR model for key metrics such as sentence accuracy, NED, and spatial IoU on the SkyReels-Text benchmark. This creates potential evaluation bias, especially because the same OCR system is also central to data curation and verification.

The main in-house benchmark is small, with only 200 diverse text samples. While other datasets are used, the most relevant font-controllable poster-editing evaluation would be more convincing with a larger held-out benchmark and clearer separation from the data sources used to build the training set.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence. Terms such as 'unprecedented control,' 'professional-grade,' and 'perfectly aligned' are not fully substantiated, and the distillation claim of over 10x speedup is not accompanied by a detailed latency/quality table.

The ablation study is useful but limited. It covers font style reference and text-region loss weight, but does not isolate the importance of plain-text conditioning, glyph-map conditioning, dataset verification thresholds, OCR quality, SAM2 masking, or the content-style decoupling strategy as a whole.

The FSR ablation is somewhat mixed: adding font style reference improves DINO style similarity and spatial alignment but substantially lowers sentence accuracy and NED. The paper explains this as OCR difficulty on stylized text, but that also highlights fragility in the reported text-fidelity metrics.

The data provenance and licensing discussion is thin. The dataset uses posters collected from design platforms, Pinterest, Amazon, and public repositories; for a paper targeting design workflows, legal and ethical constraints around training on professional poster imagery and font designs deserve clearer treatment.

The method requires substantial training resources, including roughly 512 A100-hours for the editing model and 72 A100-hours for the OCR model, which limits accessibility despite the relatively simple conditioning design.
